proposed_title: $TRUMP Fell After Melania Trump Launched $MELANIA on January 19, 2025
description_short: The Block reported an immediate 48% $TRUMP price drop; The Guardian attributed a roughly $7.5 billion market-cap loss to the ten-minute period after launch.
description_medium: The Block reported that Melania Trump launched $MELANIA on January 19, 2025, and that $TRUMP fell as much as 48% after the announcement. The Guardian reported an analyst estimate that about $7.5 billion in $TRUMP market capitalization disappeared in roughly ten minutes. Those reports describe a market reaction; they do not establish a $30 billion loss or an insider-funded pump-and-dump.
description_long: The Block reported on January 19, 2025, that Melania Trump announced the $MELANIA token and that the price of $TRUMP fell as much as 48% after the news. The Guardian reported the next day that analysts at the Kobeissi Letter estimated about $7.5 billion in $TRUMP market capitalization had been erased in roughly ten minutes. These are reported price and market-cap movements over a short period, not a finding that the launch caused a deliberate scheme. The sources do not establish that Trump family insiders sold $TRUMP holdings to finance purchases of $MELANIA, that Ran Neuner had advance knowledge and profited, or that a $30 billion loss occurred. They also use different measures and timestamps for token valuations; the specific $13 billion fully diluted peak in the original account is not carried forward without a clearly defined metric and source. This correction retains the contemporaneous launch and market-reaction reporting, with the $7.5 billion estimate attributed to the analysts quoted by The Guardian.

proposed_title: Interior Proposes Up to 34 Offshore Lease Sales in Alaska, Gulf and Pacific Planning Areas
description_short: Interior’s November 2025 draft proposed up to 34 possible lease sales in Alaska, Gulf and Pacific areas; it omitted Atlantic areas and did not issue leases.
description_medium: On November 20, 2025, Interior announced a draft 2026–2031 offshore leasing program with up to 34 potential sales across Alaska, Gulf of America and Pacific planning areas. BOEM’s proposal lists 21 Alaska, seven Gulf and six Pacific areas and omits the Atlantic. The draft was preliminary: proposed sales were not completed leases or authorization to drill.
description_long: On November 20, 2025, the Department of the Interior announced a draft proposal for its 2026–2031 National Outer Continental Shelf Oil and Gas Leasing Program. Interior described up to 34 potential sales across 21 Alaska planning areas, seven Gulf of America areas, and six Pacific areas. The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management’s first-analysis proposal is the supporting document for the specific planning areas and shows no Atlantic lease-sale areas. The announcement and proposal concern a draft planning process, not completed lease sales, issued leases, or permission to drill. This event should also remain separate from the January 20, 2025 executive order referenced in the original synopsis; the November leasing proposal does not show that the January order opened Atlantic, Pacific, or Arctic waters to leases. The corrected description keeps the later, discrete proposed-program announcement and its preliminary status. It does not forecast which areas would remain in a final program or assert environmental effects that the cited proposal does not establish.

proposed_title: The Hill Reports Allegations About Administration Efforts to Circumvent a March Deportation-Flight Order
description_short: The Hill’s July 10 report described whistleblower allegations concerning a March 15 order; it was not a finding of repeated July violations.
description_medium: The Hill reported on July 10, 2025, on whistleblower documents concerning administration officials’ response to Judge James Boasberg’s March 15 order to halt certain flights carrying Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador. The article described allegations and a contempt inquiry, not multiple July injunctions or a final contempt judgment. Its publication date is not the date of the principal alleged conduct.
description_long: The Hill’s July 10, 2025 report described a DOJ whistleblower’s account and documents concerning the administration’s response to Judge James Boasberg’s March 15 order to halt deportation flights carrying Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador. The report included allegations about DOJ official Emil Bove’s instructions and discussed contempt proceedings. It is evidence of what the whistleblower reported and of the legal inquiry, not proof that multiple new injunctions were repeatedly defied throughout July. The article’s July publication date should not be presented as the date of the underlying order or alleged conduct. The original description’s claims that flights continued throughout July after several injunctions and that federal agents repeatedly forced people onto planes are not established by this source. A later judicial probable-cause determination is also distinct from a final contempt judgment; the article notes that further proceedings were blocked on appeal. The corrected account attributes allegations to the report and identifies the March order at issue without overstating the procedural outcome.

proposed_title: Trump Fired C.Q. Brown and Pushed Out Five Other Senior Military Leaders in February 2025
description_short: Reuters reported that Trump fired Joint Chiefs Chairman C.Q. Brown and pushed out five other admirals and generals on February 21, 2025.
description_medium: Reuters reported that President Donald Trump fired Joint Chiefs Chairman Air Force General C.Q. Brown and pushed out five other admirals and generals on February 21, 2025. The report described the personnel change and Trump’s announced nominee to succeed Brown. It does not connect the removals to impeachment or January 6 testimony or establish retaliatory motive.
description_long: Reuters reported that on February 21, 2025, President Donald Trump fired Joint Chiefs Chairman Air Force General C.Q. Brown and pushed out five other admirals and generals in a major military-leadership shake-up. The report said Trump announced retired Lieutenant General Dan Caine as his nominee to replace Brown. This source supports the date, the principal decision-maker, Brown’s removal, and the broader set of senior departures. It does not say the officers were selected because of testimony in Trump’s impeachments or the January 6 investigation. It also does not substantiate the original account’s claim that Hegseth carried out the removals on January 25 or that vacancies were filled by political loyalists. The corrected description reports the personnel action without assigning an unsupported motive or extending the article’s account into claims about NATO reactions or the consequences of the changes. The Reuters account gives no political motive.

proposed_title: Flynn Registered $530,000 in 2016 Lobbying Work for a Turkish-Linked Client
description_short: AP reported that Flynn’s firm registered in March 2017 for 2016 lobbying work for Inovo BV that could have benefited Turkey.
description_medium: The Associated Press reported that Michael Flynn and his consulting firm registered with the Justice Department in March 2017 for about $530,000 in lobbying work performed before the 2016 election for Inovo BV, a Dutch company owned by Turkish businessman Ekim Alptekin. The filing said the work could be construed to have principally benefited Turkey. AP does not say the Turkish government directly paid Flynn or that he performed the work while serving as national security adviser.
description_long: The Associated Press reported in March 2017 that Michael Flynn and his consulting firm registered with the Justice Department as foreign agents for about $530,000 in lobbying work performed from August through November 2016. The client was Inovo BV, a Dutch company owned by Turkish businessman Ekim Alptekin. Flynn’s representatives stated in the filing that the work “could be construed to have principally benefited the Republic of Turkey.” AP also reported that Flynn’s firm took on the work while he was a prominent Trump campaign surrogate. This supports a disclosure about lobbying for a Turkish-linked client during the campaign followed by registration after the work period. The article does not say the Turkish government directly paid Flynn, and the work described predates his service as national security adviser. It also does not establish a specific conflict with a later U.S. policy decision or an adjudicated legal violation. The corrected wording preserves the amount and client while attributing the potential Turkish benefit to the filing.

proposed_title: White House Sought Resignations, Then Terminated Three Democratic PCLOB Members in January 2025
description_short: Reuters reported a January 23 resignation deadline; The Record later reported all three members were terminated, effective January 23 at 5 p.m.
description_medium: Reuters reported that the administration asked the three Democratic members of the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board to resign by January 23, 2025, or face termination. The Record reported on January 27 that the three had refused and were terminated, with PCLOB stating the action was effective January 23 at 5 p.m. The sources do not support a January 20 firing of every Democratic-appointed board member.
description_long: Reuters reported on January 22, 2025, that the White House had asked the three Democratic-selected members of the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board—Chair Sharon Bradford Franklin, Edward Felten, and Travis LeBlanc—to resign by the end of January 23 or face termination. The Record reported on January 27 that the three members had not resigned and that the administration terminated them; the report attributed to PCLOB an effective date of January 23 at 5 p.m. These reports establish a request followed by termination, with distinct announcement and effective dates. They do not establish that every Democratic-appointed member of the board was fired on January 20. The corrected description specifies the three members and preserves the difference between the resignation deadline, later reporting, and stated effective time. It does not characterize the board’s legal status or oversight capacity beyond what these reports document.
